title: Row continues over £140m loan to Manchester developer

input.lead: The row over public funding linked to major city centre developments could reach the Supreme Court
input.summary: The row over public funding linked to major city centre developments could reach the Supreme Court
input.evidence_text: A long-running legal battle over public loans worth £140m made by Greater Manchester Combined Authority (GMCA) to a city centre developer could be heading to the Supreme Court Landowner Aubrey Weis has applied for permission to appeal against the GMCA in the ongoing dispute over loans to so-called "special purpose vehicles" - companies set up to deliver specific development projects - linked to Renaker founder Daren Whitaker The application follows attempts to overturn the earlier ruling in hearings to the Competition Appeal Tribunal and the Court of Appeal Weis's lawyers claim the loans were unfair subsidies, but the Court of Appeal ruling in June found there had been "no error of law" in the GMCA's decision to provide them Lawyers representing Weis argued earlier this year that loans made by the GMCA to Renaker were made on a "flawed and unlawful" basis and offered "unduly favourable" interest rates The funding came from the Greater Manchester Housing Investment Loans Fund (GMHILF) and supported the Trinity Islands and New Jackson developments in Manchester city centre

title: Death of gran crushed by collapsed Shevington home wall 'was preventable'

input.lead: Warnings about the bowing wall were raised almost eight years before Clarice Berry died
input.summary: Warnings about the bowing wall were raised almost eight years before Clarice Berry died
input.evidence_text: Death of gran crushed by collapsed Shevington home wall 'was preventable' - BBC News Image source, Family handout Image caption, Clarice Berry died after the wall of her home collapsed on to her Published 17 September 2026 Concerns about a bowing wall of a rental property which collapsed and crushed a woman beneath it were reported nearly eight years before her death, a coroner found. Clarice Berry died from chest injuries suffered when the gable wall of her home in in Shevington, Wigan, collapsed on to her in July 2021, trapping her beneath the rubble. The 77-year-old was in the lean-to carport beneath the gable end of the property when the entirety of the gable wall and the upper part of the outer leaf of the end wall, weighing around 3,800kg, collapsed. In a prevention of future deaths report published on Thursday, coroner Bronia Hartley said Berry's husband reported the bowing wall nearly eight years beforehand. Hartley ruled her death could have been prevented in an inquest in July if action was taken after concerns about the wall were repeatedly raised. The home was an end-of-terrace rental property owned by landlord S&G Properties (No 2) Limited and overseen by property management company KMPM. From 2013 onwards, the property showed signs of cavity wall tie erosion, Hartley's report said. Berry reported concerns to the property's previous managing agent, but his report "fell by the wayside" when a new managing agent, Kaye Mackenzie, took over. A property manager from Kaye Mackenzie visited the property in August 2013 and recorded in his notes: "Gable wall big bulge in wall – needs urgent repointing/+rebuild." The same manager visited the property again in March 2016 and noted that the gable "needs repointing". The manager retired when Kaye Mackenzie was wound up

title: Scout Moor: Plans for onshore windfarm scaled back by a third

input.lead: Developers say the changes to the Scout Moor II scheme follow feedback from residents and consultees
input.summary: Developers say the changes to the Scout Moor II scheme follow feedback from residents and consultees
input.evidence_text: Scout Moor: Plans for onshore windfarm scaled back by a third - BBC News Image source, Cubico Image caption, The new site is planned for moorland between Rochdale and Rossendale, next to the existing Scout Moor wind farm By Richard Stead and James Fell , North West Published 17 September 2026 Developers have cut the number of turbines proposed for a major wind farm on moorland after reviewing feedback from residents and organisations. Renewable energy firm Cubico Sustainable Investments has reduced the number of proposed turbines at Scout Moor II, between Rochdale and Rossendale, from 17 to 12. The site would be next to the existing Scout Moor wind farm. The revised plans have been submitted to Rochdale and Rossendale councils and will now be subject to a further round of consultation before councillors whether to approve it. Campaign group Friends of the Moorland said it was unlikely the revisions would address all of its concerns. Steve Davison from the group said: "We need to review the plans in detail to come to a considered view but it's unlikely that all of our fundamental objections will have been addressed." Each turbine could be up to 590ft (180m) tall, making them taller than Blackpool Tower. The proposals previously prompted hundreds of objections and opponents warned of the impact on peatland, wildlife and the landscape. Peter Rowe, project lead for Scout Moor II, said the changes were a direct response to feedback from residents and other organisations. "We previously proposed 17 turbines and we're now coming down to 12," he said. "It's not about building as many turbines as possible. It's always about a balance. "We obviously want to maximise clean energy generation and secure energy generation, but equally it needs to be right for the place." Image captio

input.summary: Oldham Council has been unable to form an administration after no single party won in local elections
input.evidence_text: A council which has been without a leader since May this year has agreed to a temporary power-sharing arrangement, following months of political deadlock Oldham Council has been unable to form an administration after no political group secured enough support in local elections to assume control of the authority Senior officers had warned the continued impasse threatened the council's ability to function, with the council relying on emergency powers - a situation chief executive Shelley Kipling had described as "precarious and unprecedented" Under the plan, responsibilities that would normally fall to the council leader and cabinet will be shared between the authority's four largest groups At a full council meeting on Wednesday, councillors approved the temporary governance arrangement, designed to allow the authority to function while negotiations over council leadership continue The four parties with the largest representation on the council will undertake separate areas of responsibility

Patients were shown images associated with same-sex attraction while being given painful electric shocks in an attempt to change their sexuality. input.evidence_text: Lindow Moss peatland housing approved with 'heavy hearts' - BBC News Image caption, Members of the public and local councillors attended the meeting at Macclesfield Town Hall By Kaleigh Watterson Cheshire political reporter , Reporting from Macclesfield, Cheshire Published 17 September 2026 Plans to build 125 houses on peatland in Cheshire have been approved by councillors, who said they backed the plans "with a heavy heart". The site off Cumber Lane in Wilmslow is close to where the Lindow Man - a 2,000 year old bog body - was found in the 1980s. One councillor said he voted for the plans because the council did not "have a chance in hell of actually winning an appeal". Councillor Mark Goldsmith, who spoke against the plans, said councillors "get blamed but this is national policy in practice" while a local resident said the decision was "hugely, hugely disappointing". The government has been approached for comment. Hundreds of objections had been submitted and members of the public attended the meeting of Cheshire East's strategic planning board. David Wilson, from Protect Lindow Moss, said there were "extensive reasons" to refuse the plans. "Today you are making a decision to prevent permanent and irreversible harm to land of recognised historic and environmental importance," he said. Image caption, The site was removed from the green belt under Cheshire East Council's 2017 local plan Independent David Jefferay read a statement on behalf of the local MP, Conservative Esther McVey. title: Work to restore Manchester's Chinatown archway underway

input.lead: The gateway into Manchester's Chinatown is in need of significant repairs, the city council says
input.summary: The gateway into Manchester's Chinatown is in need of significant repairs, the city council says
input.evidence_text: Work to restore Manchester's Chinatown archway underway - BBC News Image source, Manchester City Council Image caption, The Grade II-listed landmark was a gift from Beijing to the people of Manchester Published 17 September 2026 Work has started on the restoration of a landmark archway in Manchester's Chinatown. The Grade II-listed feature was a gift from Beijing to the people of the city in the mid 1980s. The gateway into the city's Chinatown is now in need of significant repairs which is estimated to take two years to complete, Manchester City Council said. Councillor Mandie Shilton Godwin said while the arch will be missed during the work "rest assured it will be worth the wait". Image caption, The work on the archway was a "priority", said councillor Mandie Shilton Godwin The work is part of a wider regeneration of the Chinatown area. Improvements have already been carried out earlier this year to make repairs to the large pagoda, new bespoke benches have been installed, and works are planned within the month to make repairs to the smaller pagoda. Shilton Godwin, executive member for clean air, environment and transport, said the arch has been a focal point for the Chinese community in Manchester for generations and ensuring it remains standing proudly for years to come was a "priority". "We know the significance this area holds for many of our residents and that's why we are committing to further investment, ensuring that it's not only a top destination for tourists visiting Manchester, but a community that local people feel proud to live and work in." She added: "During this two-year project we know that the arch will be missed, but rest assured it will be worth the wait."
